context: Bread is bought fresh every day at 'la boulangerie'.
Ask for 'une baguette bien cuite' (well baked) or 'pas trop cuite' (lightly baked).
A classic breakfast pastry, with 'le pain au chocolat' (called 'chocolatine' in the southwest).
France has hundreds of cheeses; cheese is served before dessert.
'Beurre doux' = unsalted; 'beurre salé' = salted, typical of Brittany.
The t is silent. 'Un café au lait' = coffee with milk.
Tricky: the f is pronounced in the singular [uhf] but silent in the plural [ZUH].
'Le bœuf' (beef), 'le porc' (pork), 'le poulet' (chicken), 'l'agneau' (lamb).
Careful: 'poison' [pwah-ZOHN] with one s means poison!
'Les carottes, les tomates, les pommes de terre' (potatoes, literally 'apples of the earth').
In French 'fruit' is countable: 'je mange des fruits'.
'La pomme de terre' = potato; 'les frites' = fries.
Most fruit names are feminine in French.
'Les pâtes' is plural in French: 'les pâtes sont prêtes'.
'Une carafe d'eau' (tap water) is free in French restaurants. 'Eau gazeuse' = sparkling water.
Ordering 'un café' gets you an espresso. 'Un crème' = coffee with milk.
'Une tisane' or 'une infusion' = herbal tea.
'Un jus d'orange pressé' = freshly squeezed.

front: le vin rouge / le vin blanc
context: 'Un verre de vin' = a glass of wine; 'une bouteille' = a bottle.
'Une pression' = a draft beer, usually 25 cl ('un demi').

front: Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
pronunciation: [zhuh voo-DREH ün bah-GET, seel voo PLEH]
context: The polite way to buy anything. Start with 'Bonjour!' first: it's essential in France.

front: Je prends un café et un croissant.
pronunciation: [zhuh prahn an kah-FAY ay an krwah-SAHN]
back: I'll have a coffee and a croissant.
context: 'Je prends' (I'll take) is the natural way to order at a café.

front: Je mange du pain tous les matins.
pronunciation: [zhuh mahnzh dü PAN too lay mah-TAN]
context: Partitive article: 'du pain' = some bread (an unspecified amount). Du (m), de la (f), de l' (vowel), des (pl).
'De l'' before a vowel: de l'eau, de l'huile.

front: Je ne mange pas de viande.
context: After a negation, du/de la/des become 'de': je mange DE LA viande → je ne mange pas DE viande.
Masculine: végétarien. 'Végan(e)' is also common.
With adorer/aimer/détester, use le/la/les (the thing in general), not du/de la.
Hunger and thirst use avoir: avoir faim, avoir soif (not être).
Meals: le petit-déjeuner (breakfast), le déjeuner (lunch), le dîner (dinner).

front: On déjeune à midi et demi.
back: We have lunch at half past twelve.
context: 'On' = we in everyday speech. Lunch is an important, often long, meal in France.
Quantities take 'de' with no article: un kilo de, une bouteille de, un peu de, beaucoup de.
Also: 'C'est très bon !' Always compliment the cook in France.
Said at the start of a meal. Reply: 'Merci, vous aussi !' or 'Bon appétit !'
'Encore' = more / again. To refuse politely: 'Non merci, j'ai assez mangé.'
Also 'À votre santé !' Look people in the eye when clinking glasses.
